[MUQATIL:73:7-11/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The long daytime interval is free time for sleep and other needs; they prayed only at night, which became difficult for some.
[FARRA:v3p196#2/r10] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The long daytime activity is time to take care of one’s needs.
[FARRA:v3p196#2/r11] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | Some read سبخا with khāʾ; tasbīkh means loosening or spreading wool and cotton, as in the command “spread your cotton.”
[FARRA:v3p196#2/r12] FARRA, d. 207 · أبو زياد الكلابي | reports | Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi told al-Farra that Bedouins say “God, ease it from him” for a sick or stung person, illustrating سبخ.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p494/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Sabḥ means activity in one's needs, coming and going, and traveling back and forth.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p215/r5] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | The long daytime activity means going about, coming and going for one’s needs and occupations.
[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The day gives Muhammad and his community a long span of room for their needs and activity.
[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r10] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari says sabh and sabkh are close in sense here, both conveying ample daytime room for needs.
[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains the long daytime respite as free time, meaning sleep.

[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو معاذ | reports | Abu Muadh also explains the phrase as a long free span.
[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r8] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read the word with khāʾ as sabkhan, and this variant was explained as sleep.
[TAB-FULL:v23p376/r9] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari explains tasbikh as loosening and fluffing cotton or wool; al-Akhtal's line about cotton fluff spread by combers illustrates the usage.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p240/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The day provides a long period of free time and activity.

[ZAJJAJ:v5p240/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Sabkhan can mean a tuft of cotton; sabakhtu cotton means to fluff it, suggesting expansion and ample daytime scope.
[IBNABIHATIM:v10p3380#4/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says sabh includes various kinds of activity for one's needs and sleep.
[NAHHAS:v5p57/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar reads sabkhan with khāʾ, meaning relief and sleep; the report's tusabkhī means easing.
[SULAMI:v2p355#5/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن طاهر | reports | Ibn Tahir interprets the long daytime activity as service, turning toward God, and waiting for the arrivals of revelation.
[THALABI:v10p62/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · قراءة العامة | reports | The common reading has sabḥ with ḥāʾ; it means free time and latitude for sleep and needs, from the basic sense of moving quickly.
[THALABI:v10p62/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The root also appears in swimming and in describing a fast-running horse as sābiḥ; an unnamed poet uses sabḥ for broad movement.
[THALABI:v10p62/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar reads sabkhan with khāʾ, meaning ease, latitude, and respite; the Prophet’s phrase to ʿĀʾisha uses the verb to mean lighten.
[THALABI:v10p62/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Tasbīkh means loosening and fluffing cotton or wool; al-Akhṭal compares dogs scattering dust to loose cotton fibers.
[THALABI:v10p62/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · تغلب | reports | Taghlib contrasts sabḥ, movement and agitation, with sabkh, stillness; a prophetic saying about cooling fever with water illustrates sabkh as calming.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p126/r27] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · السدي وابن زيد | reports | Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take sabḥ as abundant supplication; in Arab usage the word also means going or traveling, as a swimmer moves through water.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p360/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Daytime offers many occupations and journeys, while night leaves the Prophet freer for worship.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p364#3/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأعرابي | reports | For the preceding daytime activity, Ibn al-Aʿrābī gives the senses of movement and livelihood.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p364#3/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth glosses the preceding phrase as leisure for the moon.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p364#3/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Daytime gives room for sleep and attending to needs, leaving the night for prayer.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:73:4-8/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Daytime is long activity in one's needs, coming and going; this urges night prayer and Quran recitation.

[JISHUMI:v10p7131/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yahya ibn Ya'mar reads سبخا with khāʾ for relief or rest; a report from Aisha cites the Prophet using the related verb for easing, and the root can mean loosening or fluffing fiber.
[JISHUMI:v10p7131/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ثعلب | reports | Tha'lab contrasts سبح as movement and agitation with سبخ as rest or stillness, citing the report to cool or ease a fever.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p254#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Sabh is movement in errands and work; its root is swift going, as in swimming.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p254#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another view takes this as daytime room for sleep and needs, leaving prayer for night.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p254#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · يحيى بن يعمر | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar reads sabkhan with khāʾ, meaning bodily rest and lightness.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p254#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet told ʿĀʾishah not to lighten a thief's case through prayer against him.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p640#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قراءة غير مسماة | reports | A reading with khāʾ instead of sīn is a metaphor from teasing apart wool fibers, like the scattering of concern and the heart through distractions.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p640#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Night is more conducive to inner agreement and recitation because people are calm and quiet; it gathers the heart and concerns, unlike daytime distractions.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p640#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Another view takes sabḥan as free time and spaciousness for sleep and tending to one's needs.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p640#2/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · قيل | reports | Another view says missed night prayer can be made up in free time during the day.

[TABRISI:73:1-10/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Sabḥ means movement or turning about, like a swimmer moving through water.
[TABRISI:73:1-10/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · يحيى ابن يعمر والضحاك | reports | Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read sabkhan with khāʾ, meaning expansion or spreading.

[TABRISI:73:8-9/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Teaching and learning do not excuse neglecting night prayer: the Prophet had greater teaching demands yet did not forgo his share.

[BURSEVI:v10p162/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says whoever sleeps through his regular night portion, or part of it, and recites it between dawn prayer and noon receives the reward as if he read it at night.
[BURSEVI:v10p162/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعض المشايخ | reports | Some shaykhs advise a sincere disciple to restore a missed regular devotion, even after a month, so the self does not become accustomed to laziness; regular litanies follow the Prophet and exemplary community.
[BURSEVI:v10p162/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · صاحب قوت القلوب | reports | Qut al-qulub says a missed voluntary wird is not legally made up like an obligatory prayer; do an equivalent when remembered as discipline and training in resolve, lest the soul get used to concessions.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | Sabh means extensive movement among daytime duties and concerns, which prevents full devotion to worship; the word originally means swift movement through water, then movement generally.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A further lexical sense is stretching: the verb can mean stretch cotton, and pieces of teased cotton are called sabāʾikh.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأخطل | reports | Al-Akhtal's verse compares hunters scattering dust to teased cotton, illustrating sabāʾikh.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن يعمر وعكرمة | reports | The Lawāmiʿ says Ibn Yaʿmar and ʿIkrima read the variant and explained it as daytime sleep to help night prayer; the author treats sleep as an implied consequence rather than the direct meaning.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse gives the external motive for night prayer, following the account of its internal motive.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One alternative takes sabh as daytime leisure and spaciousness for sleep and attending to one's needs.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another alternative says missed night worship can be made up during free daytime hours; sabh can mean free time.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The first interpretation better fits the original sense of swimming or movement and the context.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | On the free-time reading, the verse either completes the rationale for night worship because daytime allows rest, or urges preserving the vigil since it must be made up by day.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The make-up interpretation subtly evokes the alternation of night and day described in 25:62. | mentions 25:62
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن يعمر وعكرمة وابن أبيعبلة | reports | Ibn Yaʿmar, ʿIkrima, and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read sabkhan with khāʾ; one sense is a heart scattered among worldly concerns, likened to teasing wool apart.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p105#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · غير واحد | reports | Many explain the variant as relief from obligations; al-Asmaʿi says sabbakha Allah fever means God eased it, and a report uses it for lessening a supplication.
[ELMALILI:73:2-19#2/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | One reading of the long daytime activity is that worldly movement and duties obstruct the quiet and concentration available at night.
[ELMALILI:73:2-19#2/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | A second reading is that daytime is a suitable time to attend to other needs and important tasks.
[ELMALILI:73:2-19#2/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | A third, future-oriented reading offers glad tidings that after the commanded night vigil the Prophet will attain a long period of purification; the author compares the dawn image with 74:34. | mentions 74:34
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p257/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima reads “wrapped up” metaphorically as taking on the prophetic mission: expend effort in conveying it by night and day, except necessary sleep. | mentions 73:7
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p257/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | If al-Muzzammil preceded al-Muddaththir, revelation began with 96:1, then answered the accusation of madness prompted by al-Walid, soothed the Prophet after the slander, and later resumed with al-Muddaththir after he saw the angel at Hira. | mentions 96:1, 68:2, 74:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p263/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The uncoordinated sentence does not specify daytime prayers, since the five prayers were not yet prescribed according to the common view.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p263/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | One possibility is that the day verse explains why night was chosen: its prayer has deeper effect and firmer recitation, while daytime work leaves no solitude for the Prophet.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p263/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Alternatively, the verse gently justifies the night-prayer burden by allowing daytime rest after fatigue and time for the Prophet's daytime responsibilities.
[TABATABAI:73:7-8/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | Another view says daytime affords time to sleep, manage livelihood, and attend to needs, leaving the night for vigil.
[TABATABAI:73:7-8/r11] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | A further view says missed night worship can be made up in the day, as in 25:62. | mentions 25:62
[TABATABAI:73:7-8/r12] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | The interpretation of daytime as consuming work best fits the context; the make-up interpretation is linked to 25:62. | mentions 25:62
[TABATABAI:73:7-8/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Sabhan means swimming swiftly in water; a long swim by day figuratively describes immersion in livelihood concerns and varied errands.
[TABATABAI:73:7-8/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | prefers | The day is filled with many consuming occupations, leaving no free time for complete orientation toward God; therefore the Prophet should pray at night.
[ABUDAWUD:1304/r4] ABUDAWUD · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the long daytime “sabh” as a long period of free time.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p21/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · Some exegetes | reports | A common interpretation is that the Prophet’s daytime responsibilities leave little time for concentrated prayer, making tahajjud especially necessary.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p22/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | rejects | Islahi rejects the common reading that daytime busyness explains the verse: the night is inherently suited to prayer; sabḥ rarely means being busy without contextual evidence, and tawīlan fits the sense of glorification better than busyness.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p22/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The verse calls for daytime glorification as well as night prayer; the Prophet remembered God in daily activities, and transmitted supplications can turn ordinary routines into worship.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:73:5/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Besides swimming, sabḥ is metaphorically explained as rushing about among needs and activities, making journeys, or moving around; the translation adopts this sense.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:73:5/r6] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | The Prophet and, by extension, his community will spend the day earning a livelihood, conveying the Qur'an, teaching religion, and handling other tasks, so night suits worship better.
[STUDYQURAN:73:7/r1] STUDYQURAN · JJ | reports | “Lengthy affairs” means daytime responsibilities that leave no time for extensive devotion.
[STUDYQURAN:73:7/r2] STUDYQURAN · IK | reports | Alternatively, God grants an extensive span for worldly matters, implying that a part of the night should be devoted to prayer.

<<end of notes>>
